title: New study finds Europe’s digital dependence rises as US and China pull ahead
summary: Europe became more dependent on digital technologies from outside its borders between 2010 and 2023, a new policy study from the Vodafone Institute and the University of Bonn has found.
body_markdown:
**Maximilian Mayer, Professor for International Relations and Global Politics of Technology at the University of Bonn said:**


“Although European governments have implemented various policies and measures to foster digital sovereignty, their efforts have not been ambitious enough. One of the key problems is clearly the lack of strategic priorities for increasing digital capabilities and addressing digital dependencies.”


Between 2010 and 2023, the largest European percentage point increases were recorded in Finland (13.7), Sweden (7.2), Norway (6.4), Estonia (3.9), France (3.1), and Austria (2.8).


The largest European percentage point decreases were recorded in Serbia (−17.3),


Czechia


(−5.5), Poland (−4.2), and the United Kingdom (−3.5).


Europe also remained highly dependent on foreign ICT patents, limiting its ability to capture the economic and strategic benefits of technological innovation and underlining the importance of quick action.


The research shows that European countries do not share a single dependence profile. Most sit within either a “post-industrial” group, including Germany, France, Italy and the UK, or a “supply chain node” group that includes Czechia, Estonia and Poland.


These clusters possess different capabilities and vulnerabilities, meaning a uniform policy imposed across Europe is unlikely to deliver the best results.


The study also demonstrates that national trajectories can change. Serbia reduced its overall dependence substantially between 2010 and 2023, while Finland recorded the largest increase among the European countries assessed. The drivers also varied with France and Germany showing greater dependence on foreign ICT services that coincided with an increase in overall dependence.


The study recommends that European policymakers should agree shared strategic priorities as soon as possible. Furthermore, policymakers should subsequently coordinate regulation, innovation, investment and procurement across countries, sequencing short-, medium- and long-term measures to achieve Europe’s priorities.


Carefully selecting international technology partnerships and developing a long-term public narrative around the benefits of greater digital resilience are also viewed as critical for addressing Europe’s digital dependencies.


Alongside


[the study](https://www.vodafone-institut.de/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/digital-dependencies.pdf) , an


[interactive Digital Dependence Index website](https://www.digitaldependence.eu/) allows policymakers, researchers, journalists, businesses and the public to compare countries and regions, examine changes over time and explore the underlying data. It also includes an AI-supported tool designed to help users navigate the dataset and its policy context.
